bc_lynx.blurb: Lynx is one large boulder in the forest above Arrow Lake, in the Cat bouldering zone near Castlegar, and it holds fourteen problems. The grade spread is wide: one very easy problem, a handful of V1 and V2 lines, a few around V3 and V4, and three hard problems at V6 and V7. It suits a mixed group, since beginners and strong boulderers both find something, and the harder lines are sustained and pumpy. Several moderates and open projects make it a good place to spend a whole session on a single rock. Only a few minutes separate it from the neighbouring Wildcat boulders, so combining the two is easy.
bc_lynx.approach: From the Broadwater Road pullout, cross the road and follow the flagged trail into the trees, with some lesser boulders off to the right. When you reach a big cairn, bear right and continue for roughly a minute to reach the boulder.

bc_china_grove.blurb: China Grove is a compact crag of about 70 feet tucked among the small eastern crags of Skaha Bluffs, above Skaha Lake near Penticton. It has fourteen routes, split evenly between sport and trad, running from easy 5.6 climbing through the 5.10s and into 5.11 and 5.12 territory. The rock gives crimpy, technical climbing rather than big pulls. It catches morning sun and falls into shade later in the day, which helps on warm afternoons. Being away from the busy main walls, it tends to be quieter, though the scramble to reach it takes a little more effort than the lower crags.
bc_china_grove.approach: Take the trail that starts below the upper parking lot and passes Daycare and Diamondback. At Elusive Edge, fork right toward Grassy Glades. China Grove sits a short detour beyond, reached by a rift or gully near Grassy Glades.

bc_yellow_sling_wall.blurb: Yellow Sling Wall is one of the cliffs at Kinnaird Bluffs, a long-established climbing area on the edge of Castlegar in the West Kootenays. It faces south and holds fourteen routes, eight trad and six sport. The grade range is broad, starting at easy 5.4 and 5.5 terrain, building through a solid group of 5.9s and 5.10s, and finishing with several 5.11 and 5.12 lines plus one 5.13. That mix gives trad climbers crack lines and moderate routes to warm up on, while sport leaders have harder bolted options. With its southern exposure it gets plenty of sun and is a good choice outside the hottest part of summer.
bc_yellow_sling_wall.approach: Park on Sahlstrom Road and walk the trail to Open Book Wall, then continue east past a large gully. Yellow Sling Wall is the next cliff along.

bc_tulip_falls.blurb: Tulip Falls is a scenic crag above Arrow Lake inside Syringa Provincial Park, west of Castlegar in the West Kootenays. It has fourteen routes, ten sport and four trad, on two walls: one beside the waterfall that stays in shade, and one in the trees that faces southwest. This is a crag for stronger climbers: only a couple of routes are around 5.9, most sit at 5.11, and a good number reach 5.12. The climbing is steep and sustained, with water-worn features and pockets. The shade makes it a pleasant choice on hot summer days, and the setting near the lake and a beach adds to the appeal.
bc_tulip_falls.parking_note: Drive Broadwater Road to Syringa Provincial Park, stay right on the Deer Park forest road and follow it for about 4 km. Park in the pullout on the right.

bc_backside.blurb: Backside is the quieter sibling of the main Frontside crag at Roche Lake, a forested spot roughly 40 minutes from Kamloops. It has fourteen routes, mostly sport with a few trad lines, ranging from 5.8 up to hard 5.11 and low 5.12. The routes are shorter than those on the Frontside, so it works well as an alternative when the main crag is busy. Climbers often have it to themselves, and the surroundings are old Douglas-fir forest with the occasional owl. Late summer, fall and spring are the comfortable seasons, since mosquitoes can be bothersome in high summer.

bc_exchamsiks.blurb: Exchamsiks is a gneiss sport crag beside the highway near Terrace in northwest British Columbia, a short way west of the Exchamsiks River bridge. All fourteen routes are bolted, with a friendly spread from 5.7 to 5.12: a pair each at 5.7, 5.8 and 5.9, a cluster of 5.10s, and a few harder lines above. The wall faces south to southwest and takes strong sun through the middle of the day, while a breeze off the river helps keep insects down. One overhanging section dries quickly and can stay climbable when the weather is wet elsewhere.

bc_lonely_island.blurb: Lonely Island is a small beginner-oriented sport crag in the Lonely Crags above Kelowna. Its fourteen routes are short, bolted slab and vertical lines, mostly 5.4 to 5.7 with a couple at 5.8, and each finishes at a two-bolt anchor. A 30 m rope covers every line. The banded, multi-coloured rock climbs more like Skaha or Cedar than its neighbours. The wall faces east, catching the early sun and falling into shade by mid-afternoon, which makes it comfortable on warm days. Some rock is loose in places, so a helmet is wise. It is a good spot for learning to lead and clean anchors.

bc_a2_wall.blurb: A2 Wall is one of the cliffs of Aberdeen Columns, a basalt crack-climbing area in the hills east of Vernon in the Okanagan. All fourteen routes are trad, mostly 5.8 to 5.10 with a solid group of 5.10s and a few 5.11s. Compared with the main columns it is steeper, longer and wider, and it feels burlier, with more greenery around it. It is worth a half-day visit, with wide views across the valley lakes toward the Monashee Mountains. Bring a full trad rack, as protection is by cams and nuts.

_conflicts.bc_tulip_falls: Stored rock is syenite; https://www.mountainproject.com/area/114308868/tulip-falls, https://sendage.com/area/tulip-falls-bc-canada and https://squamishclimbingmagazine.ca/?p=12042 all say gneiss.
_conflicts.bc_lynx: Stored rock is granite; https://www.mountainproject.com/area/114543656/lynx and https://www.mountainproject.com/area/114543652/cat-boulders describe the Cat area as gneiss.
